purpose: Structured catalog of every reviewer check pulled from best-practices/ and references/ in the sales-letter-method skill. Used by Phase 4 regression tests and future eval automation to score letters and reviewer outputs against named claims.

assertions.claim: The file reads as one complete argument top to bottom. A cold reader understands the whole thing in one pass.
assertions.applies_when: any best-practice file, reference file, reviewer output, or final letter copy is being shipped
assertions.fail_pattern: Reader stumbles on a section. Something is missing they need to follow the logic. A section feels foreign (research log notes, internal-only framing, codes nobody outside the team would recognise).

assertions.claim: The language reads at Singapore third-grade English. A smart non-marketer understands every line.
assertions.fail_pattern: Jargon (load-bearing element, quarantine the ask), codes (F1, A1, A2), industry words (controls, the ask, pattern attestation), sentences over 20 words, passive voice, anything that makes the reader feel talked down to or excluded.

assertions.claim: Q1 was applied before Q2. Structure was fixed first, then language.
assertions.applies_when: reviewer is checking whether a file or letter has been properly polished
assertions.fail_pattern: Pretty sentences sitting inside a broken argument.

assertions.claim: Reviewer applied general copywriting judgment beyond the named checks in any one best-practice file.
assertions.applies_when: reviewer is grading a draft against a specific best-practice file
assertions.fail_pattern: Reviewer went silent on a real problem because the best-practice file did not name a check for it.

assertions.claim: Letter uses only the components that fit the offer. No components were forced in.
assertions.fail_pattern: All 12 components present in a letter where only 8 fit. The letter feels bloated.

assertions.claim: Every promise in the letter has a number, a name, or a timeframe attached.
assertions.fail_pattern: Vague phrases like 'great returns', 'more leads', 'better results' with no number behind them.

assertions.claim: Every proof element is real. Sourced from a real client, a real credential, or a real sample.
assertions.applies_when: any letter has a proof stack
assertions.fail_pattern: Made-up testimonial, invented result, fake screenshot.

assertions.claim: Scarcity, if present, names a real capacity limit. No countdown timers and no fake 'only X left' lines.
assertions.fail_pattern: Countdown timer, manufactured deadline, heavy pressure tactics for a high-ticket consulting offer.

assertions.claim: The letter has a guarantee block.
assertions.fail_pattern: Long letter with no risk-reversal at all.

assertions.claim: The letter has both an FAQ block and at least one P.S.
assertions.fail_pattern: FAQ skipped because 'it looks long'. P.S. dropped because it feels old-fashioned. Eight out of eight modern competitor pages skip both.

assertions.claim: The letter passed the de-AI pass before delivery.
assertions.applies_when: any letter is about to ship
assertions.fail_pattern: AI-shaped language patterns still present in the final draft.

assertions.claim: The letter does not name a price on the page.
assertions.applies_when: letter is a lead-gen funnel page
assertions.fail_pattern: Price disclosed on the page. That belongs in the copywriting skill, not this one.

assertions.claim: The user approved the letter before it was written to disk.
assertions.applies_when: agent is about to save the letter to a client folder
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter written to disk without explicit user approval (y / save / ship it).

assertions.claim: Letter avoids the 'force all 12 components' trap. Only the components that fit the offer are present.
assertions.fail_pattern: Drafter packs every component into a letter that needed only 8.

assertions.claim: Letter avoids the vague-promise trap. Every benefit promise has a specific number or timeframe behind it.
assertions.fail_pattern: 'More leads' instead of '12 booked calls a month'.

assertions.claim: Headline names something only this offer can claim. A competitor could not paste it onto their page.
assertions.fail_pattern: Headline could be used by any of ten other businesses in the same space.

assertions.claim: Proof points to buyers who look like the reader, not to the operator's own greatness.
assertions.fail_pattern: Proof reads as 'look how good we are' instead of 'look at people like you who won'.

assertions.claim: CTA button uses outcome language, not 'Submit', 'Send', or 'Click Here'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Button says 'Submit' or 'Send' instead of naming what the buyer gets.

assertions.claim: Letter avoids the heavy-urgency trap. No countdown timers, no red exclamation marks.
assertions.fail_pattern: Countdown timer or 'only 24 hours left' framing on a high-ticket consulting offer.

assertions.claim: FAQ block is present.
assertions.fail_pattern: FAQ skipped because the writer thought it would look long.

assertions.claim: Specific numbers survived the de-AI pass. They were re-injected if the sweep stripped them.
assertions.applies_when: letter has been through the de-AI pass
assertions.fail_pattern: Numbers in the original draft were lost after Sweep 8 and never put back.

assertions.claim: Phase 0.7 mechanism and offer architecture document was a required input for Phase 1.
assertions.fail_pattern: Drafter improvised the mechanism name. Letter dismisses competitors at category level ('most agents fail to follow up') instead of naming real alternatives.

assertions.claim: Letter has at least one P.S. block.
assertions.fail_pattern: Modern long letter with no P.S. at all. Eight out of eight modern competitor pages drop the P.S.

assertions.claim: If the letter is 1,500 words or more, there are 2 or more P.S. blocks.
assertions.fail_pattern: One P.S. in a long letter unless it carries the whole price-and-order detail (the Halbert way).

assertions.claim: If there are multiple P.S. blocks, each does a different job from the named list (price-and-order, deadline-restate, bonus-reminder, guarantee, what-if-I'm-not-ready, if-you-do-nothing, personal-promise).
assertions.applies_when: letter has more than one P.S.
assertions.fail_pattern: Two P.S. notes doing the same thing.

assertions.claim: If there is only one P.S., it is either the price-and-order P.S. or the 'what if I'm not ready' P.S.
assertions.fail_pattern: Single P.S. carrying a weak generic sign-off instead of the price-and-order or fear-handler job.

assertions.claim: The P.S. carries a sharp promise, a deadline, a guarantee, or a fear-handler. It is not a generic sign-off.
assertions.fail_pattern: P.S. added because 'we should have one' with no real job.

assertions.claim: Writer can point at each P.S. and name which job it does from the list.
assertions.applies_when: writer is defending the P.S. choices
assertions.fail_pattern: Writer cannot name the job.

assertions.claim: Headline contains a specific fact. A number, a process step, an identity question, or a small story moment.
assertions.fail_pattern: Headline is a benefit claim ('get more leads', 'scale your agency') with no fact behind it.

assertions.claim: Writer can point at the fact in the headline and name what kind it is (specific-number, process, identity-question, small-moment story, damaging-admission).
assertions.fail_pattern: Writer cannot name the fact type.

assertions.claim: Numbers in the headline are exact, not rounded. '$13,995' beats '$14,000'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Rounded numbers that feel estimated, like '$14,000' or 'big returns'.

assertions.claim: Headline does not lead with the benefit. The benefit is implied by the fact, not stated.
assertions.fail_pattern: 'Get more leads' as the headline. The reader has heard that claim a hundred times.

assertions.claim: A cold reader feels curious enough after the headline to read line two.
assertions.fail_pattern: Headline is boring, generic, or over-promising. Reader does not lean in.

assertions.claim: If you removed every adjective from the headline, it would still work. The fact carries the load.
assertions.fail_pattern: Padded headline that uses adjectives to do the fact's job. Ogilvy did not write 'the amazingly quiet Rolls-Royce'.

assertions.claim: There is at least one damaging admission in the first screen of the letter.
assertions.fail_pattern: Every claim is positive and curated. No vulnerability anchor. Eight out of eight modern competitor letters admit nothing.

assertions.claim: The admission is real and checkable. The reader could in theory verify it.
assertions.fail_pattern: Admission reads as theatre. Reader cannot verify it after the fact.

assertions.claim: Admission is written in plain words, not marketing language. No 'radical transparency' framing.
assertions.fail_pattern: Claim of honesty ('we are honest and transparent') instead of demonstration of honesty (giving something up).

assertions.claim: The admission is paired with a strong move. A guarantee, risk reversal, deferred ask, or proof stack sits right after it.
assertions.fail_pattern: Admission sits alone with no recovery move. Karbo paired his price admission with a 31-day no-cash-check guarantee.

assertions.claim: The admission has real bite. Scored 1 to 5, where 1 is a soft hedge ('we're not perfect') and 5 is Karbo telling you the markup.
assertions.fail_pattern: Soft hedge that gives up no real ground.

assertions.claim: Writer admits one thing, not five. Multiple admissions in a row sound like a confession scene.
assertions.fail_pattern: Three or more admissions stacked. Sounds like an apology letter.

assertions.claim: All five critical boundaries are clean. No jump at Headline-to-Sub, Lead-to-Pain, Pain-to-Mechanism, Mechanism-to-Proof, or CTA-to-P.S.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 2 Stitcher is running or reviewer is grading transitions
assertions.fail_pattern: A section ends and the next one opens on a new topic with no bridge. Reader hits a wall.

assertions.claim: Each section opens by echoing, escalating, pivoting, or answering the prior section. Writer can name which bridge pattern is in use.
assertions.fail_pattern: Section opens cold with no anchor back to what came before.

assertions.claim: No transitional filler phrases. Cut 'Now let's talk about', 'Moving on', 'Next up'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Filler phrases at section boundaries.

assertions.claim: No over-bridging. No section starts with a two-sentence recap of the section before.
assertions.fail_pattern: Section opens with 'as we just discussed' and a summary of the prior section.

assertions.claim: Overall flow scored 1 to 5. Reader can go top to bottom without stumbling. Each stumble costs a point.
assertions.fail_pattern: Reader stumbles multiple times. Letter does not sound like one voice.

assertions.claim: Cohesion ratio across all section boundaries. 'Continuous' plus 'bridge' must be at least 85% to pass, 95% for strong, 100% for premium.
assertions.fail_pattern: More than 15% of boundaries are marked as a jump.

assertions.claim: Letter has a P.S. Modern competitor set drops the P.S. eight times out of eight. Including one puts the letter ahead of the field.
assertions.applies_when: long-form letter is being graded against the modern field
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter is field-average. No P.S. like the other eight modern letters.

assertions.claim: Mechanism is named. Not 'our system', not 'vast network'. A real name like 'The Entry Price Pattern' or '7 Sales Laws'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Mechanism is described in generic language. Reader cannot repeat the name.

assertions.claim: There is a damaging admission somewhere in the letter. Zero out of eight modern competitors do this.
assertions.applies_when: long-form letter is being graded against the modern field
assertions.fail_pattern: No admission at all. Every claim is positive.

assertions.claim: Guarantee is real, not 'satisfaction promise' hand-waving. Specific reversal like refund window, do-not-pay-if-X, or conditional pricing.
assertions.fail_pattern: Guarantee is a soft behavioral promise with no structural reversal.

assertions.claim: Letter is not inheriting Syncom template moves without earning them. 'I will NEVER' stacks and X-bullet checklists work, but if five out of eight competitors already use them, the letter sounds like everyone else's.
assertions.fail_pattern: Triple-negative and pain-persona checklist used without adapting to this offer's voice.

assertions.claim: If the founder credibility anchor were cut, the letter would still work. The letter is not one removed testimonial away from being broken.
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter collapses without the founder bio. All proof is upstream of one person.

assertions.claim: All ten canonical objections are addressed somewhere, inline or in the FAQ.
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter skips three or more of the ten worries.

assertions.claim: At least one qualification block with testable conditions is present. Not 'for serious people only' but a money, stage, time, or situation filter.
assertions.fail_pattern: No filter at all, or filter is vague flattery.

assertions.claim: Letter carries at least five different trust signal types, distributed across three or more components.
assertions.fail_pattern: All proof stacked in one testimonials section. Reader can skim past it.

assertions.claim: Mechanism uses at least one of the four justification patterns (cause-and-effect, contrast, first-principles, constraint).
assertions.fail_pattern: Mechanism is named but never justified. Reader cannot say why it beats the old way.

assertions.claim: Cohesion holds. No more than 15% of section boundaries are jumps, and zero of the five critical boundaries are jumps.
assertions.fail_pattern: Any jump at H-to-S, S-to-L, L-to-P, P-to-M, or CTA-to-PS.

assertions.claim: P.S. block is present for letters 1,500 words or longer.
assertions.applies_when: letter word count is 1,500 or more
assertions.fail_pattern: Long letter ships with no P.S.

assertions.claim: Narrator point-of-view holds end to end. No drift between the avatar, peer, operator, or other registers.
assertions.fail_pattern: Mid-letter drift. Opens as the operator, mid-letter slips into a peer voice, closes as a journalist.

assertions.claim: Letter includes a FAQ section covering the five core objections (Time, Money, Authority, Stall, Preference).
assertions.fail_pattern: FAQ missing. One of four universal gaps modern competitors leave open.

assertions.claim: Letter includes a P.S. line that handles the final fear at the bottom of the page.
assertions.fail_pattern: P.S. missing. One of four universal gaps.

assertions.claim: Letter includes a stacked guarantee with two or three variants together, not just one.
assertions.applies_when: any long-form letter with a guarantee section
assertions.fail_pattern: One thin guarantee where two or three would have closed the deal.

assertions.claim: Letter includes an integrity tie-down: a rhetorical commitment right before the mechanism reveal.
assertions.fail_pattern: Mechanism reveal lands without the tie-down. Reader's trust has not been re-anchored before the pitch.

assertions.claim: Letter does NOT use heavy countdown timers, fake 'only 2 spots left', fake testimonials, unhonoured guarantees, or 'act NOW' urgency.
assertions.fail_pattern: Any of the named manipulation tactics present.

assertions.claim: Pain Cycle (Components 2-3) is in first-person with short sentences (5-10 words), opens on one concrete scene, and ends with stuck-ness.
assertions.fail_pattern: Pain prose in third person, long compound sentences, no concrete opening scene, no ending in stuck-ness.

assertions.claim: Discovery and Proof (Components 4-6) show results first, name the product second. Discovery comes via life circumstance, not 'I researched online'.
assertions.applies_when: letter has a Discovery or Proof section
assertions.fail_pattern: Product name leads, result follows. Discovery feels engineered.

assertions.claim: Mechanism Reveal (Component 5) is 3 to 4 sentences for the core reveal. If it takes more than four sentences, it is still a hypothesis.
assertions.fail_pattern: Mechanism reveal balloons into a whitepaper.

assertions.claim: Transformation section follows the 30% physical / 70% emotional split. Timeline structure ('Day 3', 'Week 2'), outside validation, ends with the new normal.
assertions.applies_when: letter has a Transformation or Outcome section
assertions.fail_pattern: All-physical results list, no emotional layer, no outside validation, vague words like 'better' or 'improved'.

assertions.claim: No component is more than 20% above its word budget.
assertions.applies_when: any letter is being graded against component budgets
assertions.fail_pattern: Pain Cycle balloons into whining. Mechanism reveal balloons into a whitepaper. CTA rehashes the body.

assertions.claim: Lead type is named. Writer can point at the opener and say which of the six Schwartz lead types it is (offer, promise, problem-solution, big-secret, proclamation, story).
assertions.fail_pattern: Writer cannot name the lead type. Opener is improvised without a pattern behind it.

assertions.claim: Opener names a real avatar. First line uses the reader's name or names the segment tightly enough that the wrong reader walks away. Not 'Dear friend'.
assertions.fail_pattern: 'Dear friend' or 'Dear entrepreneur'. Mass-mailer feel.

assertions.claim: First sentence is short. Five words or fewer if possible. Ten max.
assertions.fail_pattern: Long opening sentence kills the slippery slide before it starts.

assertions.claim: Each sentence sets up the next. Read three sentences cold. Reader cannot stop after sentence two without feeling pulled to sentence three.
assertions.fail_pattern: Slippery slide breaks. Reader can quit at sentence two with no pull forward.

assertions.claim: Lead type matches reader awareness. Cold reader gets story or big-secret. Warm reader gets promise or offer.
assertions.fail_pattern: Cold reader hits an offer lead and bounces.

assertions.claim: Letter has a guarantee at all. A long letter with no risk-reversal is a real gap.
assertions.fail_pattern: No guarantee block. Reader bears all the risk of the call, the read, or the buy.

assertions.claim: Guarantee is structural, not just verbal. Karbo's 'I won't cash your check' is structural. 'Satisfaction guaranteed' is verbal.
assertions.fail_pattern: Guarantee is a vague verbal promise. No specific structural reversal behind it.

assertions.claim: Guarantee is specific. Numbers, timeframes, named outcomes. Vague guarantees like 'you'll love it' count as no guarantee.
assertions.fail_pattern: Guarantee uses soft language with no concrete commitment.

assertions.claim: Guarantee matches the funnel. Money-back on a no-price page is a mismatch. No-pitch on a paid product page is a mismatch.
assertions.fail_pattern: Guarantee type does not fit the funnel stage.

assertions.claim: If two guarantees are stacked, each does a different job. Do not stack two that say the same thing.
assertions.applies_when: letter stacks more than one guarantee
assertions.fail_pattern: Two guarantees doing the same job. Padding, not strength.

assertions.claim: Mechanism sentence names three to five real brand or product alternatives, not 'most agents' or 'most coaches'.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.7 mechanism architecture is being reviewed
assertions.fail_pattern: Dismisses competitors at category level. 'Most coaches fail to follow up' instead of naming Endowus, T-bills, structured notes.

assertions.claim: Each alternative's failure mode is structural. Names a math, process, incentive, or system reason a competitor would feel obligated to defend.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.7 mechanism architecture is being reviewed
assertions.fail_pattern: Failure mode reads as a vibe instead of a verifiable structural reason.

assertions.claim: MAGIC name's container word survives the rules. Not a saturated noun ('system', 'framework', 'blueprint'). Two or three syllables. Pronounceable cold.
assertions.fail_pattern: Container word is generic and forgettable.

assertions.claim: Letter addresses one avatar segment, not 'primarily segment 2 with some 3'.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.7 bouquet narrowing is being reviewed
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter tries to address everyone and ends up specific to nobody.

assertions.claim: Mechanism section uses at least one of the four justification patterns: cause-and-effect, contrast, first-principles, or constraint acknowledgment.
assertions.fail_pattern: Mechanism named but never justified.

assertions.claim: Justification gives a verifiable cause-and-effect reason. Not 'it works because it works'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Justification is a re-assertion of the claim.

assertions.claim: Justification word count matches the letter length table. 800 words: 50 to 80 justification words. 1,200: 80 to 150. 1,800-plus: 150 to 250.
assertions.fail_pattern: Justification is too short to land, or so long it becomes a whitepaper.

assertions.claim: After reading Component 5, the reader can say in one sentence why this beats the old way.
assertions.fail_pattern: Reader closes the section and cannot articulate the why.

assertions.claim: Each of the ten worries is handled somewhere. Inline, in the FAQ, or in the P.S.
assertions.applies_when: any long letter is being graded
assertions.fail_pattern: Five or more worries unhandled. Time, money, authority, stall, preference, fit, risk, effort, prior failure, or post-click reality left open.

assertions.claim: Fit worry is handled in the lead or first 200 words.
assertions.fail_pattern: Wrong-fit readers stay reading deep into the letter before realising it is not for them. Half of them leave first.

assertions.claim: Risk worry is handled by a real guarantee, not just a line that says 'you're safe'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Slogan-as-guarantee. 'We've got you covered'.

assertions.claim: Prior-failure worry is named in the body, with a clear reason this is different.
assertions.applies_when: audience has likely tried something similar before
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter ignores that the reader tried something before and it did not work.

assertions.claim: Money worry is handled in the body or in the P.S., not skipped.
assertions.fail_pattern: Money worry is left to the reader's imagination.

assertions.claim: FAQ block carries the leftover five worries (time, authority, stall, preference, plus one more), each in two sentences.
assertions.fail_pattern: FAQ is a dump of worries that should have been killed inline.

assertions.claim: P.S. carries one worry on purpose, not a generic sign-off.
assertions.fail_pattern: P.S. is a generic 'looking forward to working with you' line.

assertions.claim: Each handled worry gives a reason or a proof, not just a claim.
assertions.fail_pattern: Worry is named but the answer is a slogan with no specific reason or proof.

assertions.claim: Letter has a qualification block at all. A letter with no filter reads as 'we will take anyone's money'.
assertions.fail_pattern: No filter anywhere in the letter.

assertions.claim: Filter lines are testable. Each one is a thing the reader can tick yes or no on with no thinking. Money, stage, time, or situation.
assertions.fail_pattern: 'For ambitious people' or 'for serious agents'. Nothing testable.

assertions.claim: There is at least one real 'not for you' line. Saying who the offer is not for is the strongest trust signal.
assertions.fail_pattern: Only includes 'who this is for' lines. No 'who this is not for'.

assertions.claim: Filter matches the headline. Headline does not promise 'anyone can do this' while the body says 'only for X'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Headline and filter contradict each other. Reader catches the lie.

assertions.claim: Tone reads as honest filtering, not gatekeeping theatre. Honest reads like a founder protecting delivery. Theatre reads like a doorman.
assertions.fail_pattern: Filter feels performed. Insults pretending to be filters ('not for lazy people').

assertions.claim: For consulting-level offers, a readiness check sits before the CTA. Reframes the click as 'am I ready?' not 'do I want this?'
assertions.applies_when: letter is for a consulting-level offer
assertions.fail_pattern: No readiness check. CTA fires as a pure want-question.

assertions.claim: Letter carries at least five different KINDS of trust signal. Count the kinds, not the instances. Nine testimonials equals one kind.
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter leans on one signal type only. Usually testimonials. Mono-signal stacks read as curated highlight reels.

assertions.claim: Trust signals are spread across at least three different sections of the letter. Not stacked in one proof block.
assertions.fail_pattern: All proof crammed into one testimonials block. One section to skim past.

assertions.claim: At least one trust signal is a verifiable fact or a demonstration. Not a testimonial.
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter has zero demonstration of process or machinery. All proof is testimonial or credential.

assertions.claim: Numbers in the letter are specific, not rounded. '$2.00 single, $1.00 each additional' beats '100s of clients'.
assertions.fail_pattern: Round numbers signal estimate. '500+ closings', '$2M+ managed' read as guesses.

assertions.claim: Every confident claim sits next to a credibility signal (a constraint, a context, a condition) within three sentences.
assertions.fail_pattern: Bold outcome claim sits unpaired. No constraint, no context, no condition near it.

assertions.claim: Letter has no 'claimed honesty without demonstrated honesty'. No 'we are transparent' or 'no hidden fees' without a real giveaway behind it.
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter asserts the trait of honesty and moves on. No damaging admission behind the claim.

assertions.claim: The CAN bucket lists at least five concrete claims, each with the proof source named.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.5 claim audit is being graded
assertions.fail_pattern: CAN bucket has fewer than five claims or no proof source named.

assertions.claim: The CANNOT bucket names every competitor mentioned in the offer or buyer-profile docs and marks them off-limits for brand-name comparison.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.5 claim audit is being graded
assertions.fail_pattern: Competitors named in source docs are missing from the CANNOT list.

assertions.claim: For health, money, or legal verticals, every CANNOT entry maps to the rule it would break (ad-platform policy, regulator, or platform-specific).
assertions.applies_when: offer is in a regulated space (health, money, legal)
assertions.fail_pattern: CANNOT entries lack the source rule. Drafter cannot tell which rule the claim breaks.

assertions.claim: The NEEDS CAREFUL WORDING bucket has at least one entry, or the auditor has written one sentence on why none apply.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.5 claim audit is being graded
assertions.fail_pattern: Bucket is empty with no explanation. Auditor skipped the careful-wording category.

assertions.claim: The claim audit document fits one screen.
assertions.applies_when: Phase 0.5 claim audit is being handed to Phase 1 drafters
assertions.fail_pattern: Document sprawls past one screen. Drafters will not use it as a hard constraint.

assertions.claim: The three polish passes ran in the named order: copy-editing Sweep 8 (de-AI), unslop with the long-form-sales-letter profile, then brand-voice-guardian.
assertions.fail_pattern: Polish passes skipped or run out of order.

assertions.claim: The sales-letter-auditor agent ran in an isolated context window with no generation history.
assertions.fail_pattern: Auditor ran in the same session that wrote the letter. Step is wasted.

assertions.claim: The auditor returned one of four verdicts: SHIP, HOLD-minor fixes, HOLD-blockers present, or DO NOT SHIP.
assertions.fail_pattern: Verdict is hedged ('mostly good'). Not one of the four named verdicts.

assertions.claim: Every blocker from a HOLD or DO NOT SHIP verdict has been fixed before the auditor was spawned again.
assertions.applies_when: auditor returned HOLD or DO NOT SHIP
assertions.fail_pattern: Letter shipped with blockers still in place, or auditor was re-spawned without fixes.

assertions.claim: All five pre-ship lenses are PASS. Any FAIL has a documented fix applied. Any WEAK has an operator override reason logged.
assertions.fail_pattern: FAIL on UMP clarity, identity-layer depth, headline-body coherence, concentration sharpness, or CTA structural completeness, with no fix applied.

vague_assertions_flagged.note: Original source says 'every confident claim paired with a credibility signal within 3 sentences'. The phrase 'confident claim' is fuzzy. Marked score-1-5 instead of yes/no so reviewer judgment can fill the gap.
'Honest filtering vs gatekeeping theatre' is taste-driven. Marked score-1-5 with a fail-pattern anchor.
'Reader stumbles' is subjective. Tied to a count rubric (each stumble = minus one point) to anchor it.
'Reader can articulate the why' depends on the reader. Marked score-1-5; pair with a buyer-lens reviewer who reads cold.

schema_notes: default_severity uses 'critical / important / nice-to-have'. Critical = ship-blocker (regulatory red flag, fabricated proof, missing hard-rule core component, brand-doc conflict, violation of the 9 critical rules). Important = significant performance hit but letter can still ship. Nice-to-have = polish-level.
score_type 'binary-with-justification' was reserved but not used in this pass — every vague check was demoted to score-1-5 with an anchor instead.

reviewer_fit slugs come from best-practices/_index.md and phase-3-reviewer-stack.md: buyer-lens, copy-chief, self-contained, eval-halbert, eval-sales-letter. 'all' means every reviewer in the Phase 3 stack should score it.
applies_when conditions are plain English so Phase 4 regression tests can branch without parsing codes.

2026-05-27 calibration pass: severity audited against best-practices/_critical-rules.md (the 9 hard rules) as ground truth. 32 critical assertions demoted to important. 0 important promoted to critical. Bias was toward demotion — original distribution was 59/56/3, calibrated to 27/88/3.
